name: States of matter and how structure explains properties

terms.definition: Solid, liquid and gas; the particle model shows particles as small solid spheres.
terms.examiner: Limitations: particles are not solid spheres and there are no forces shown.

terms.definition: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
terms.examiner: The stronger the forces between particles, the higher the melting point.

terms.definition: Substances made of molecules with strong covalent bonds within them but weak intermolecular forces between them, so they have low melting and boiling points.
terms.examiner: It is the intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds.

terms.definition: Weak forces between molecules; they increase with the size of the molecule.
terms.examiner: Larger molecules have higher boiling points.

terms.definition: A very large molecule of atoms linked by strong covalent bonds; intermolecular forces are fairly strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.
Many atoms joined by covalent bonds in a lattice, such as diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide, with very high melting points.
terms.examiner: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken.

terms.definition: A mixture of a metal with other elements; harder than the pure metal because the different-sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide.
terms.examiner: Pure metals are too soft for many uses.
